title: #261: Reality Fracture First Impressions
scale: No grades given; this is a first-impressions episode, and the show normally grades in its full set review.

cards.take: Seems pretty good, because a -2 that makes a 2/2 and surveils 1 is usually a better use of Jace than the base -3 draw a card.
Looks really strong: targeting your own planeswalker makes it hard to blow out, and a high-loyalty Jace can turn it into a two-mana deal-eight.
A seven-mana 7/5 trampler with two modes on entry; the ramp deck will often cast it on turn six, and it would have been a rare a few years ago.
Quite good, mainly because two +1/+1 counters plus trample is a strong mode, while the flyer-kill and ritual modes are good situationally.
Usually wary of expensive creatures without immediate impact, but expects this to draw a card right away fairly often thanks to enter-and-gain-life effects.
Could go either way: a three-mana dork that only makes green is unexciting, but gaining four or five life over a game is real, even in ramp decks.
A nice common life-gain payoff that trades a point of toughness for Ward 1, which is slightly unfavorable but fine, and it pairs well with Medic's Kitesail.
Gives GW an evasive attacker that gains life every turn, growing Hortimancer and triggering Bloombrute right away.
Predicted to be one of the best commons: better than Murdock's Crusade because the good mode gains life and the draw mode works like cycling when there is no target.
A four-mana 3/4 flyer that pumps another attacker each combat, or gives it a permanent counter after a scry or surveil; a pretty good aggressive WU payoff.
A nice take on the two-mana blue defender that can attack once you've scried or surveilled, which WU and Jace tokens enable easily.
Reads weak but gives steady filtering and surveil triggers, then burns for two, and surveiling into flashback cards may make it worth a card; could be sneaky good or among the worst in the set.
A good gold card: four mana for two 2/2s up front, and the expensive flashback later makes much bigger tokens in the self-mill deck.
A strange design that plays like a three-mana 2/4 you can pump at threshold, with a cute combo alongside Tetsuko Umezawa for big unblockable hits.
A nice removal spell: a top-or-bottom tuck that costs a mana less than usual and punishes opponents who keep the card on top.
A pretty good UR gold card: a 2/4 that makes hasty flying Thopters off noncreature spells.
Has been good for decades and is exactly what UR wants, helping it keep pace and move big blockers out of the way.
A pretty good common for UR: a cheap cantrip that triggers spell payoffs twice and nets real card advantage through flashback.
A really good WB attrition gold card that gains life on deaths and turns sacrifices into counters and menace.
A clearly pushed gold card: unconditional removal of any nonland permanent plus counters on your team.
Basically a better, correctly-rare version of an equipment that was a top attrition card in The Hobbit: removal on entry plus +2/+1; expected to be one of the best rares.
Good on its own, since it comes in and kills or badly shrinks a creature, which is ideal for BG midrange.
A solid standalone BG body with menace whose mill-four and land-return give value and graveyard synergy.
A pretty good common flashback card: a 4/4 trampler now and another later for six.
Another very strong gold card: three damage to any target plus three life on entry, then a +2/+1 equip that gets cheaper on countered creatures.
Part of the strong-gold-card trend, handing out +1/+1 counters as creatures enter in RW aggro.
Likes the look of this 2/4 that makes attackers unblockable and gives planeswalkers a big Leviathan ultimate, but unsure how good it is.
A confident banger: a 4/4 flyer that fights on entry, and its GUU cost stops green ramp decks from easily splashing it.
Would be playable even without basic landcycling, since six mana for three 2/2s plus Empower Jace 2 is solid, and cycling makes it flexible.
Likely to be overlooked as clunky six-damage removal, but the +1/+1 counter adds stats to the board and landcycling makes it the second-best of the cycle.

format.summary: A complex, full-size set with 10 color pairs, built around paired Multiverse/Echoverse legends and the Empower Jace mechanic. The five allied pairs are Strixhaven-style schools with clear enabler/payoff themes, while the enemy pairs are looser traditional archetypes; drafts expected to split roughly 60/40 between schools and enemy pairs, unlike Lorwyn Eclipsed's roughly 90/10. Gold cards and charms look notably pushed.
format.speed: Not directly stated. Aggressive decks exist (UB-free RW, WU, BR aggro), alongside ramp and midrange; how often players should attack opposing Jace tokens versus racing is an open question.

colors.take: Has strong commons like Surgical Precision and supports life gain, and landcycling spells like Hexhaven Battalion.
Has strong blue staples like Unsummon plus scry/surveil tools, and anchors Empower Jace and the spells decks.
Supports attrition and self-mill; Lich's Relic stands out as a top rare.
Has removal like Awaken the Inferno and supports pinging and spells aggro.
Supports ramp, life gain and counters, with flashback threats like Bestial Incursion.

pairs.take: Konstrari: a true dedicated ramp deck using Heartwood mana tokens to power out big payoffs like Craftwork Crusher a turn early.
Stingerquill: aggro that cares about noncombat damage and pinging the opponent, death by a thousand cuts, with Grim Repriser recursion.
Vigorbloom: a creature deck built on life gain, with +1/+1 counters as a secondary theme; key pieces are Bloombrute, Unflinching Hortimancer and Medic's Kitesail.
Fatehold: aggro that cares about scrying and surveilling, with plenty of triggers available, including Jace's -1.
Theorix: self-mill feeding flashback and threshold (seven or more cards in the graveyard) payoffs like Recursive Recruitment.

Spellslingers; one of the cooler-looking decks, helped by Unsummon, flashback and cheap card-draw commons. It is easy to build wrong by mixing red aggressive and blue controlling spell payoffs, so commit to one.
Attrition, with strong gold cards: sacrifice fodder, discard creatures and 1.5-for-1 effects that grind out an advantage.
Midrange, wanting cards that are good on their own, with some graveyard and flashback flavor.
Aggro with +1/+1 counters and strong gold cards like Warrior's Blades.
Empower Jace; more a multicolor shell that splashes the Way enchantments to stack abilities on a Jace token, with Mind Meanderer a standout.

mechanics.name: Echoed pairs (Multiverse/Echoverse legends)
mechanics.take: Legends appear as two differently colored versions. Packs show a full pair plus one extra half-pair, which hides what the neighboring drafter took.

mechanics.name: Empower Jace
mechanics.take: Adds loyalty to a Jace token (-1 surveil 1, -3 draw a card). Roughly, Empower Jace 3 is about a card, but the value arrives over time and the token can be attacked or burned.

mechanics.name: Way enchantments
mechanics.take: A double uncommon cycle, two per color, that empowers Jace and grants your planeswalkers new abilities, often better than the base ones.

mechanics.name: Prepared (school hybrid cards)
mechanics.take: Each school's hybrid uncommon becomes prepared with a shared school-specific spell, keeping each archetype's strategy consistent.

mechanics.name: Flashback and threshold
mechanics.take: Support graveyard strategies and help self-mill, UR spells and value cards like Eye of Jace.

mechanics.name: Charms and gold cards
mechanics.take: Noticeably pushed and stronger than Strixhaven's.

mechanics.name: Fixing lands
mechanics.take: A cycle of duals that enter untapped with a planeswalker, a common choose-a-color land, and spells with basic landcycling for any basic.

advice: Expect roughly 60% of decks to be allied school pairs, but enemy pairs are viable if you read signals and know how to assemble archetypes like midrange or aggro yourself.
Prioritize the pushed gold uncommons and charms.
Treat Empower Jace 3 as roughly a card, but remember the draw is spread over turns and the token can be attacked.
Consider attacking opposing Jace tokens versus simply racing; this is still an open question.
In UR, commit to either red-based spells aggro or blue-based control, not a mix of both payoffs.
Surgical Precision is likely one of the best commons.
Value landcyclers that are playable on their own, like Hexhaven Battalion and Awaken the Inferno.
Don't overlook stats added to the board, like the counter on Awaken the Inferno.
